analysis.one_liner: Adds $15 an hour to essential workers' pay during public health emergencies, with the federal government reimbursing employers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2021 with 20 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared public health emergency, the bill would require employers to pay workers on the government's essential-infrastructure list an extra $15 an hour on top of their regular pay. Employers who pay the premium would get a dollar-for-dollar federal payroll tax credit, refundable in cash if it exceeds what they owe, so the cost lands on the Treasury rather than on businesses. The bill never moved past its initial committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Essential workers — the bill defines them by the CISA critical-infrastructure memorandum, which covers not only health care staff but also grocery, food-processing, transit, trucking, and other frontline jobs. They would take home an extra $15 for every hour worked during an emergency period.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must pay essential employees their regular rate plus $15 an hour during an emergency period, with violations treated as unpaid overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S3].
Employers receive a credit against payroll taxes equal to 100% of the required premium pay, and any credit exceeding their payroll tax liability is refunded in cash [S3].
The bill makes the Social Security trust funds whole by transferring from the general fund any revenue lost to the credit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. Because the credit reimburses employers 100% of the premium and is refundable, the entire cost of the wage boost is carried by the Treasury through the general fund.

drawbacks.text: The definition of 'essential employee' follows the CISA critical-infrastructure memorandum, which covers a very wide swath of occupations beyond health care, so the fiscal cost during a nationwide emergency like COVID-19 could be enormous [S3].

Employers bear no net cost because the credit reimburses them in full and refunds any excess, making the program a pure federal wage subsidy with no employer cost-sharing and little incentive to limit premium hours [S3].
The requirement attaches to any 'emergency period' as defined in Social Security Act section 1135(g), not just COVID-19, so it would apply again in future declared public health emergencies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to workers is real and immediate: $15 more per hour when the country is in an emergency and they are still showing up. The honest cost concern is fiscal design — because the federal government fully reimburses and even refunds employers, every dollar of the raise comes out of the Treasury, and the broad essential-worker definition means the price tag in a pandemic-scale emergency would be very large. A supporter would defend that as the right party to pay; a skeptic would note the bill contains no offset and no employer contribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2021 and sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees, and neither ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Essential Pay for Essential Workers Act on February 2, 2021 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee, and within Ways and Means to the Health Subcommittee [S5].
Twenty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no hearing result, no floor vote. The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of essential workers are better off because the bill died — they never faced the wage mandate, even a fully reimbursed one, and the Treasury avoided an open-ended emergency spending program. Essential workers, who would have received the pay, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of essential workers and the Treasury

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill mandating $15-an-hour emergency premium pay for essential workers with a full employer tax credit.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax credit
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup; it sat in committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it received no further action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the split could have been tested [S4].

industries.note: During emergencies they would have been required to add $15 an hour to frontline pay, but the federal credit reimburses the full cost, so the premium would function as free federal help with recruitment and retention during staffing shortages [S3].
These large employers of 'essential' workers would have received a fully refundable federal subsidy covering the mandated wage increase for their frontline staff [S3].
